title: Foxtrot Network: The shadowy gang recruiting teen killers across Europe
description: Young guns for hire - the teenage hitmen recruited to kill across EuropeImage source, Swedish PoliceImage caption, Atilla Azimov posing with a gun thr
body: Young guns for hire - the teenage hitmen recruited to kill across EuropeImage source, Swedish PoliceImage caption, Atilla Azimov posing with a gun three months before he killed Murad AbdelkaderByDaniel SandfordUK correspondentIn a Stockholm suburb a man dressed in black appeared out of the winter night. Carrying a handgun, he approached 20-year-old Murad Abdelkader, a student on his way back from a shift at McDonald's. The gunman opened fire, shooting again and again as he approached his target. He fired the last shot into his victim's head as he lay helpless on the ground. The killer was 18-year-old Atilla Azimov. On that February night last year, he had killed the wrong man.He had done it for money - hired by the Foxtrot Network, an organised crime group with links to the Iranian regime which has become notorious for its violence-as-a-service (VaaS) tactics.Image source, Swedish PoliceImage caption, Atilla Azimov, seen in CCTV images and after his arrest, was jailed for life for the mistaken killingSince 2022, the Foxtrot Network is thought to have been responsible for about 35 murders as well as a number of attacks and attempted attacks on Israeli targets in Europe including two involving explosives and hand grenades.The gang recruits teenagers to carry out the attacks for cash, but it almost never has to pay out as they often get caught.Like Johannes Natland, a Norwegian teenager who was convicted of conspiracy to murder by a jury at the Old Bailey in London on Wednesday for a planned killing in West Yorkshire.According to Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, the Europol group set up to tackle the problem, the teenage hitmen are recruited on social media, and are given their instructions in a "gamified" way, imitating how computer games work.Andy Kraag, the head of Europol's European Serious and Organised Crime Centre, calls it the "calculated outsourcing of murder" to vulnerable young people.OTF GRIMM currently involves 11 countries affected by the VaaS phenomenon - Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.Image source, Swedish PoliceImage caption, Rawa Majid, the leader of Foxtrot, pictured with Ali Shehad Ahmed, who is believed to be part of the networkThe leader of the Foxtrot Network, Rawa Majid, has fled Sweden and his later operating base in Turkey, and is now based in the Iranian capital Tehran. Police believe some of the VaaS attacks have been carried out for the Iranian regime, including a hand grenade attack on the Israeli embassy in Copenhagen, though other attacks are part of Foxtrot's drugs turf wars.Diamant Salihu, an investigative journalist for the Swedish broadcaster SVT, has been researching Foxtrot and its Iranian links for three years."The regime is ordering the leader of the Foxtrot Network to instigate his network to commit attacks against the Iranian regime's enemies," he said."It can be dissidents, journalists that are in the opposition against the regime, and it can also be Israeli targets."The links to the Iranian regime started after October 2023 when Majid fled to Tehran, Salihu said."He had to make a deal to be able to live freely in Iran, under condition that he and his network work for the regime."The Foxtrot Network and Majid were sanctioned by the UK government, external in April 2025.That was the month after the arrest of Natland, who was 18 at the time. He had flown in to carry out a hit on behalf of Foxtrot somewhere near Huddersfield. Image source, Counter Terrorism PolicingImage caption, Teenage hitman Johannes Natland posing with cash he had been givenThe Natland case illustrates how the VaaS system works. Natland is the son of two journalists in Stavanger and had a comfortable upbringing, but he drifted into drugs and developed psychosis, ending up spending time in rehab and a short period in a children's home. There he met another teenager who used the online handle UnknownHustler.It was UnknownHustler who first sent Natland the online request for someone to carry out a hit in the UK - "Killing in England 270k" (270,000 Norwegian kroner is about £21,000). It had come from another teenager with the handle Generalen. Generalen - who was 16 at the time and had spent the last three years living in a children's home - subsequently recruited Natland for the hit.Natland was then passed on to a Foxtrot member with the online username Agent 47, which is borrowed from the Hitman game franchise. Swedish police have accused Ali Shehad Ahmed, who is close to the Foxtrot leader Majid, of being Agent 47.Agent 47 booked Natland's one way ticket to Manchester Airport, and helped him through the process of getting an emergency passport. Using the messaging app Signal, he guided Natland at every stage of his journey before handing him on to a logistics man with the username "1".Treating Natland a bit like a character in a computer game, "1" sent him a map and videos showing him where to find the guns hidden in woodland in Huddersfield, and then another video showing him how to access a stash of cash hidden in the undergrowth near a foot tunnel.Once Natland was installed in his Huddersfield hotel with the weapons, Agent 47 messaged him again: "We have much to do tomorrow."Natland was arrested the next morning. He had not yet been told who he was to kill, and counterterrorism detectives are still trying to work out whether it was to be a criminal hit or a political one carried out for Iran.The teenager who recruited Natland - Generalen - was prolific. As well as hiring Natland as a hitman he had also recruited at least two people who carried out murders in Sweden. They were Azimov, who is serving a life sentence for killing the wrong man, and a 17-year-old who shot dead Ahmed Zamzam in Lund, south Sweden, three and a half weeks earlier.Neither of the killers got paid, because they were both caught. Salihu said this was part of how Foxtrot worked."They don't care at all if the teenagers get caught. Because when they get caught, they cannot ask for money that they have been offered, and we see no examples of money being paid to these young killers," he said."It has been a deliberate policy to recruit younger and younger teenagers because they don't think about the consequences of getting caught, and they are more willing to take the risks."Generalen was eventually stopped because he was trying to arrange the murder of the 14-year-old son of a Norwegian police officer. He recruited a 15-year-old and a 17-year-old to carry out the knife attack, but the 15-year-old told the police. When Generalen was arrested detectives found details of the Huddersfield murder plot on his phone that led to British police arresting Natland just in time.Generalen was convicted in May and is serving a 14-year-prison sentence.Image source, Iraq National Intelligence ServiceImage caption, Ali Shehad Ahmed was arrested in Iraq and Sweden has requested his extraditionOTF GRIMM has had some successes in the 15 months since it was set up. Police have made more than 280 arrests including a few key suspects.One of the most important arrests was that of Ahmed, who is thought to be Agent 47.He was detained in the Kurdish city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq, and is currently subject to an extradition request to Sweden.The Swedish deputy national police commissioner Stefan Hector said they were "constantly expanding our co-operation with other countries" and showing organised criminals "they cannot feel safe anywhere in the world".In May, Mohamed "Moewgli" Mohdhi, a former rapper described by Swedish police as a "central actor" in Foxtrot, was arrested in Tunisia.But Majid himself remains out of reach in Iran."He's still active," Salihu said. "And as long as this network is active we will still continue, I fear, to see attacks on the enemies of the Iranian regime."It is not yet clear the extent to which the arrests have degraded Foxtrot's ability to operate, but other groups - including Foxtrot's rivals the Dalen Network - have already adopted the VaaS method of recruiting vulnerable teenagers for murders, so the danger is still very present. It spread quickly from Sweden across Scandinavia and northern Europe and, as the Natland case shows, reached the UK last year.

schema.headline: Foxtrot Network: The shadowy gang recruiting teen killers across Europe

title: Newspaper headlines: Chancellor 'warns' supermarkets and 'own goal'
description: The Sunday Telegraph reports, external that Chancellor John Healey has warned of more "cost-of-living pain" because of the Iran war, but says he'll be
body: The Sunday Telegraph reports, external that Chancellor John Healey has warned of more "cost-of-living pain" because of the Iran war, but says he'll be "hands on" to protect the public. He's written in the paper that he'll be watching closely for any suggestion of people being "ripped off" when shopping for essential groceries, or filling up their car at the petrol pump.According to the Sunday Times, external, Nigel Farage struck a deal to return as the leader of Reform UK months before the 2024 General Election much earlier than he has said. Sources have told the paper there were negotiations in March and April 2024. A Reform UK spokesman is quoted dismissing the report as misinformation, or mischief-making.A couple of the papers carry accounts of what happened when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta last week. The Sunday Times says, external the border crossing "had been brewing for weeks". The paper adds there have been claims the event has been linked to posts on social media promising an easy path to Europe.The front page of The Mail on Sunday, external features a photograph of a Spanish soldier checking on two men who have collapsed on the beach at Ceuta due to exhausation. The Sun on Sunday, external has spoken one of those who crossed from Morocco. Twenty-six-year-old Mohammed Mounsessef says he swam for 40 minutes, wearing a backpack, describing the journey as "very very dangerous". The paper says he expressed a desire to come to the UK, to change his life."It's been a hellish week for Gianni Infantino" writes the Sunday Telegraph, external as the fallout continues from the Fifa president's failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup. The Sunday Times says, external he's "battling to save his job" as his opponents step up efforts to force him to resign. "Time to go" declares the Sunday Mirror, external. The Observer says, external Gianni Infantino's journey from "unassailable power to abject humiliation seems almost complete", summing up with the headline "own goal".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: Chancellor 'warns' supermarkets and 'own goal'

title: Love Island UK has a problem, say fans - 'there's not much love'
description: Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi were crowned winners of the latest UK seriesByNaomi ClarkeBBC Newsbeat
body: Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi were crowned winners of the latest UK seriesByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatWhat's your dream Love Island series on paper?  Some watch for the heartwarming romances, like Molly-Mae Hague and Tommy Fury falling for each other back in 2019, while others prefer intense dramas - we see you 2022 winners Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu and Davide Sanclimenti.Others tune in for exciting challenges like Snog, Marry, Pie or the ones which literally send heart rates soaring. For most, it's a mix of all of the above, and it's a balance TV producers have been trying to strike for years with the original UK series, as well as a host of spin-offs and international editions. It's no secret that Love Island UK linear viewing figures have dropped from their 2019 heyday, with streaming and social media becoming more of a focus. Across the pond the US edition has been reaching new heights, with the latest eighth series ranked as the number one reality show for five weeks in the States across all streaming platforms, according to its streamer Peacock. , externalIt also had an injection of star power as US celebrity fans, including Lizzo, Demi Lovato and Kesha, sent messages of support to the finalists, while rapper Megan Thee Stallion has become a regular guest. BBC Newsbeat has been speaking to fans, commentators and an ex-Islander to see what they feel the UK edition could learn from the US version to regain its spark. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The latest US series was ranked as the number one reality show in the States across all streaming platformsThe 13th series of the UK show ended on Monday, with Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi crowned the winners.The final drew in an average audience of 1.1m viewers across all devices, including streaming, according to its broadcaster ITV, but this was a notable drop from last year's, which had an overnight audience of 1.3m.  By comparison, series five in 2019 broke the show's viewing records with 6m tuning in to an episode post Casa Amor, and that year's final had the highest average audience to date.However, ITV say this 2019 figure was a consolidated number reached once it "had received all the data post final" and said it do not yet have an "equitable" figure for Series 13.According to the network, more than 60% of its audience now engage with the show through streaming and the latest series, as well as its companion shows Aftersun and The Debrief, have had more than 180 million streams on ITVX.Content creator Sarel, known for her Love Island debriefs to her 1.2m followers on TikTok, feels the biggest issue with the most recent UK series is "there hasn't been much love" between the couples, so she wasn't rooting for anyone at the end.And while she knows people watch it for the drama and conversations it sparks, she thinks those are just "added extras" and the romances should be at the centre of the show."I want somebody to fall in love. I love stories where we get the butterfly moments," she says. "Where you had your Indiyah [Polack] and your Dami [Hope] when they ran to each other, or you had couples like Molly-Mae and Tommy." She thinks that's an aspect which the US version has been getting right, as it feels like "everyone who is in there actually fancies one another" and there is "no box" they have to fit into. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Traitors UK winner Aaron Evans was on series six of Love Island USASomeone from the UK who chose to go on the US version is Aaron Evans, but this wasn't his first reality series as he was one of three winners on the first series of The Traitors UK.He feels the US edition's success is helped by having "fresh eyes" on the format and the show having "so much social media presence", which makes it "highly engaging".Stats given to Newsbeat by TikTok - which called Love Island "one of the most influential entertainment franchises" on the app - suggest he's not wrong.During the latest series, the hashtag #LoveIsland was mentioned in 123,000 posts in the UK, with #LoveIslandUK featuring in 88,000.While in the US, #LoveIsland appeared in 1.09m posts and #LoveIslandUSA was tagged in 502,000 posts.That said, the US population is nearly five times the size of the UK's. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, American celebrities like Megan Thee Stallion are among fans of the US edition US entertainment journalist Carly Thomas says executive producers have told her they look for ways to "bring in the US audience", be that through social media, challenges and the islanders they choose."I think for the US audience, we love to just relate and connect with people," Thomas, who works for The Hollywood Reporter, says. She also feels the US edition wants to "push the limits" of the islanders with intense challenges and viewers "love to see how far they'll go", including rapper Megan Thee Stallion hosting one which saw them sit on cakes and throw them at each other. Love Island USA has not been all smooth sailing, though. Contestants in last year's series faced relentless online bullying which forced the show to broadcast a statement saying it does not tolerate "cyberbullying, harassment or hate". The show insists it takes duty of care seriously.The US version runs for six weeks once a year, while the UK summer edition typically airs across eight weeks. There is also now an additional series in the UK throughout the year, with a winter edition airing in 2020 and 2023, which has now been succeeded by All Stars.The finale of the third All Stars version, which sees ex-islanders return to the villa, attracted about 910,000 viewers earlier this year.Image source, HandoutImage caption, Superfan Dami Amoo says the UK series is starting to feel "overproduced"During the most recent UK series, producers tried to get hearts racing, and TikTok numbers up, by introducing some new twists.A few islanders were summoned for a sleepover at a different villa before Casa Amor, and for the first time, only three couples were in the final after two pairs got dramatically dumped.Some fans have appreciated the changes, while others, like Sarel, feel they didn't land. Love Island superfan Dami Amoo, who has watched every episode of the UK, US and All Star editions, says the UK series is starting to feel "overproduced"."I do think it's been on a steady decline because they're trying to give us what we want, but then they're overdoing it and then they're taking away the classic [elements]."She thinks this may have been due to budget constraints, but missed the islanders going on exciting dates and taking part in "fun activities or games" where you see their personalities more.Amoo, 28, also thinks you can really see the impact of investment in the US version, which was aired almost simultaneously with the latest UK edition."They've invested so much into the props, the games and all of these brands are part of the actual production," she says."Whereas the UK version, it seems like they're just on an island somewhere just doing it on their own."You don't get a lot of hype, we don't get British celebrities contributing to the discussions."'Everything's just very American'The US edition has been able to bring in revenue by becoming a major space for advertising, external, with numerous content partners and more than 1,000 media partners, according to Peacock.Evans isn't surprised by the US version capitalising on brand partnerships, saying  "everything's bigger, everything's brighter, everything's just very American".So as the sun sets on another run of Love Island series, what could UK producers do ahead of the next launch? Superfan Dami thinks "they should really get some real fans in the production room"."The people that do the debriefs online, people who engage on Twitter, they should get us in a room and we tell them what we really, really want." An ITV spokesperson told Newsbeat "reaction of the fans is at the heart of the show as seen in public votes and including opinions as part of the challenges."They added Love Island UK "continues to wield huge cultural relevance, both in the UK and in the USA" and to date it has had "over 2bn streams on ITVX and remains the biggest 16-34 show in commercial television".Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Srosh Khan and Jack Gray. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Love Island UK has a problem, say fans - 'there's not much love'

title: EU calls emergency meeting to discuss Ceuta migrant crossings
description: The European Union will hold emergency talks on Tuesday to discuss the migration crisis in Ceuta after tense exchanges between Spain and other member
body: The European Union will hold emergency talks on Tuesday to discuss the migration crisis in Ceuta after tense exchanges between Spain and other member states.Twenty-two member states issued a joint letter calling for co-ordinated action and the strengthening of the EU's external borders, after some 60,000 migrants entered the Spanish enclave from Morocco. Spain condemned "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction to the crisis after Italy suspended the EU's border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain - a move backed by Finland and Denmark. Officials say almost all those who reached Ceuta on 30 July have returned, while deaths from the surge in crossings had risen to at least 67. The EU members' letter addresses concerns around "hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible," adding that the perception "would encourage further attempts, undermine confidence in our common migration policy and have repercussions for all Member States". Leaders of the Netherlands, Finland and Belgium are among 22 signatures on the letter, addressed to EU President Antonio Costa, president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and Taoiseach Michael Martin, as Ireland currently holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union. In a separate letter to von der Leyen, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments.He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any "unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe" in less than 48 hours.While most had shown "support and solidarity", Sánchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest", and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.

schema.headline: EU calls emergency meeting to discuss Ceuta migrant crossings

title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight fire
description: The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world.Originally from Spa
body: The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world.Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes.She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires  of 2019-20, which razed a combined area about the size of the UK.Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters.Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations.This is where Australia has an advantage.The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years.Using Indigenous ecological knowledge – a plant's colour and scent, for example, or the shade cover of trees - he can verify information in the satellite images from Yebra's team."She had all this amazing data, but there was no translation to what it meant on the ground, so it was kind of useless," he explains."But through an Indigenous perspective, it was not useless. It was a map that could guide you through the country and, if you understood it, take you directly into a place that is ready to burn."For Webster, assessing the land involves him "literally digging and going underground," he says."We're looking at the subsurface level and then everything from that up beyond the canopy."Yebra said there was a "remarkable agreement" between Webster's local knowledge and the satellite data, demonstrating the combined value of Indigenous expertise and Western science.Her team now hopes to get more funding for the project, and work with Indigenous communities to co-design plans to protect the land and manage fires.For Webster, it's about "allowing our mother – the planet Earth – a voice again".Another example of ancient wisdom influencing modern techniques can be found in the way Australia fights fire with fire.Cultural burning refers to a longstanding practice by Indigenous Australians to manage the environment while also maintaining a deep, spiritual connection to the land.Part of it is lighting "cool fires": small, controlled blazes that create a patchy landscape, so fuel does not build up in one area."In Europe, there is no such cultural aspect to this kind of landscape planning," Yebra says.Wildfire scientists in Spain have blamed a massive build-up of fuel for the blazes currently devastating the country."It is difficult to watch what is happening in Spain, but it is not surprising," Yebra says. "Particularly as climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme fire weather across southern Europe."She believes Europe, facing its worst wildfires in decades, could benefit from Australia's firefighting experience."We have decades of experience living with large and high-intensity bushfires," she says. "One of the biggest changes we are seeing in bushfire management is a shift from simply reacting to fires towards anticipating risk and acting earlier."The earlier we can identify risk or detect an ignition, the more options firefighters have."Webster says a key lesson the world could learn from Australia is "don't sit back and wait"."The longer you leave it, the more fuel there is to burn, so the fire is naturally going to be bigger and harder to extinguish," he says."Indigenous people always knew that, so we burnt continuously all the time. That way there was no fuel for big fires."The practice of lighting cool fires dates back 60,000 years. Part of Webster's role is to assess the area before one is lit, looking for natural signs of oil and water in the landscape so that the blaze remains under control."All the answers are in the environment," he says. "There's a sweet spot in the middle where there's enough water to slow that fire down but there's enough oil to push that fire on."A more modern tactic used across Australia is a prescribed burn, also known as a hazard reduction burn. These carefully planned, often large-scale fires are usually carried out during cooler months, and are increasingly being adopted in parts of Europe.It's an approach that has become especially vital in the "urban fringes", says superintendent Andrew Shurety from Fire and Rescue NSW.As Australia's population grows and suburbs expand, more people are moving closer to bushland, making hazard burns firefighters' "main mitigating factor that we try to do to reduce the risk of bushfires because we know they're going to come".The problem, Shurety points out, is that longer fire seasons and more rain during cooler months shortens the window that such burns can be carried out.Starving a fire of fuel is also the idea behind "backburning", a widely accepted practice in Australia where a blaze is deliberately lit ahead of a main fire to strip out the vegetation and try to stop it from spreading.This approach is also being increasingly adopted overseas - as Queensland firefighter Damian Hatfield found out.When he travelled to Alberta, Canada with a contingent of Australian firefighters to help tackle the country's worst wildfires on record, backburning was not widely used. A year later, things had shifted."Backburning was definitely much more at the forefront when I returned in 2024," he says, with Canadian firefighters showing "no hesitation" to include the approach in their operations.Drones have also transformed how Australia deals with bushfires, says Trent Curtin, from the Rural Fire Service in NSW - particularly in recent years."The local crews arrive, send a drone up quickly, have a look at where the fire is and how it's progressing, get some intelligence and make decisions before we can even get our large helicopters or other aircraft down," Curtin explains.Drones also deliver heavy gear to crews on the ground, start blazes for backburning operations and help assess the damage caused by fires.Back at Yebra's centre, the team's work is particularly timely with weather forecasters predicting a super El Nino this summer - which could increase the probability of extreme heat, drought and bushfires."Our next fire season is looking like it's going to be a bad one," Yebra says.That concern is shared by Jason Heffernan, chief officer of the Country Fire Authority in Australia's southeastern state of Victoria. Here, the memories of 2009's Black Saturday bushfires – the country's deadliest on record – loom large."For this summer coming, we're bracing for what could be something extremely significant," Heffernan says. Even in the broader scheme of things, he notes that local fire seasons are starting earlier and lasting longer. "Unfortunately for Australia", he adds, "our environment is designed to burn."But as the world braces for wildfires that are more frequent and intense, Heffernan also believes "we must take a global perspective"."No fire service can do this on their own and the key is to have formal and trusted networks," he says - as well as national and international resource-sharing arrangements.One of the challenges as a fire chief, he explains, is knowing when to ask for help - too late and the benefits will be lost, but too early and resources might be wasted.Such a call was made just earlier this week, when France sent its first-ever request for help from Australian firefighters. Two dozen crew and several aircraft will be deployed as France battles record-breaking wildfires amid a prolonged summer heatwave.Australia regularly sends specialist teams to the US and Canada, and vice versa, with many requests for what's known as "arduous fire crews": those who have fought fires in rugged and remote areas.There are far fewer requests from Europe, Heffernan says - but this may change as "the global fire community is becoming more connected".As he points out, while forests and climates vary across the globe, "we're seeing bushfires occur in parts of the world that never had bushfires before".

schema.headline: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight fire

title: Why more men in their 20s are having vasectomies
description: I had a vasectomy in my 20s after the trauma of my sons' birthsImage source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex West says he remembers the months after the
body: I had a vasectomy in my 20s after the trauma of my sons' birthsImage source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex West says he remembers the months after the births of his two sons as "grey"ByGeorge SandemanAlex West was left harrowed by the difficult labour his wife endured for their first child. When it came to their second, he hoped for a much smoother arrival.The birth did go better for his wife - but not for him. "I had a panic attack and broke down. I hadn't been able to - I didn't have the ability to - process that," Alex says.Unresolved trauma from his wife's first labour and his subsequent postnatal depression meant Alex didn't want to continue with the couple's plan to have four children.He remembers the months after the births of his two sons as "grey" - life was devoid of colour and filled with people telling him that being a father must be a fantastic experience."I didn't feel this love and connection that everybody says I should have," Alex says.Not wanting to repeat the experience, he and his wife agreed to stop at two kids. Given he was the driving force behind the decision, he felt it was "wrong to put the onus on my wife" to take a contraceptive.So like thousands more men in England have done in recent years, Alex chose to have a vasectomy.The procedure involves the cutting and then clamping or sealing of the vas deferens, a tube on each testicle that carries sperm to the urethra. It's colloquially known as the snip.Figure caption, How a vasectomy worksSome 26,385 vasectomies were performed at hospitals and clinics during 2024-25, according to data compiled by NHS England. This was 16% more than in 2023-24.Men aged 35-39 had more procedures than any other age group, about 8,400 in 2024-25.There had also been a slight rise on the previous year in younger men choosing to have the snip - about 950 vasectomies were performed on men aged under 30 in England during 2024-25.Fears about pregnancyAlex, a mortgage broker, decided in his late 20s to have the procedure but his NHS doctor urged him to wait until he turned 30 in case he changed his mind.When the appointment came in May 2024, he and his wife took the train from their Kent home to the London clinic.The procedure was quick and painless says Alex, now 33. "I put my headphones on and I listened to about three songs before they said it was all done."Ridiculous - crazy quick."Image source, Sam KnightImage caption, Sam Knight decided to have a vasectomy after a woman he was dating became pregnantSam Knight, who's from the US, says he knew he didn't want to have children."I was putting myself in situations where kids could be a potential option and that really started to, kind of, freak me out," Sam says. When his then-partner became pregnant, she chose to have an abortion and Sam, aged 22 at the time, felt a change was needed."[I had] a realisation of this thing that I've put somebody through and I just didn't want that to ever happen again."He contacted a urology clinic in New York and, like Alex, had to explain to clinicians why he wanted a vasectomy. Sam was advised the procedure should be treated as permanent, as it can only be reversed in some circumstances.Strict criteria for reversals Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them."We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just to… make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision." She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one. The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.Image source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex and his wife initially planned to have four kids but after careful consideration stopped at two"I've devoted my life to this and, to me, parenting is something you also devote your life to," Sam says. "I just don't have the mental space or the time to do that, or even the desire to."Sam, now 25, says he envies those who do want to become parents because the experience "clearly has" beauty and love in it. But adds, "I find that in music and art and these things that I do."The procedure in 2024 and the aftercare cost Sam, who was still on his family's health insurance policy, about $1,200 (£849) in total.He's among fewer than 1% of men in the US aged 18-29 who have ever had a vasectomy, according to the National Survey of Family Growth, which analysed the responses of about 4,000 men in 2022-23. Men in their mid to late 40s were most likely to have had one -15% said they had.Sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent Sam experienced one bout of excruciating pain a week after the procedure, a known but uncommon side effect of vasectomies according to Dr Salkeld, but that subsided after a few hours.He doesn't think this should put other men off having a vasectomy. "Overall, it is worth the money and it is worth the pain," he says.Another man told us the sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent - particularly how his children might turn out - drove him to have a vasectomy aged 27.Back in Kent, the decision to get the snip felt like the fairest and most effective form of contraception available to Alex and his wife.It was something they considered carefully over several months, knowing they no longer wanted more children."I absolutely adore my children," Alex says, particularly now they are old enough to play football with."If I had added more to the team, it wouldn't have been the right thing for me."Get in touchWe are interested in hearing from men who have had a vasectomy reversal. What prompted your decision?

schema.headline: Why more men in their 20s are having vasectomies

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Josh Kerr wins Saturday night scrap in Glasgow
description: There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Gla
body: There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight. Not his childhood pal and Scotland team-mate Jake Wightman. Not the Australian prodigy Cam Myers. Not the former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot. This Commonwealth Games men's mile was his race, in his country, in front of his people. This gold medal really meant something. Kerr's explosion of joy after he crossed the line and swaddled himself in a Saltire - having conducted the crowd during his final few strides - made that clear. And so did his halting attempts to sing along with Flower of Scotland, the 28-year-old repeatedly stopping to bite his lip before wiping away tears from each eye. "We rush through these moments so quickly," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland, having spent the best part of 45 minutes doing selfies and signatures. "So I was just telling myself to slow down. "In my head, I was flashing through all the hard moments and realising that I've come a long way. And to have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different. Not many times in my career I'll ever have that."When Kerr crossed the line, the clock showed he was almost eight seconds slower than when running the fastest time ever for the mile in London last month. Three minutes 54.12 seconds.What it didn't show was that for three of the four laps, this was more rammy than race.   Emerging between fireworks, Kerr had strutted out on to the track, spinning a bottle, and allowed his 12 rivals to sprint away. Only once they checked and began to run back did he stretch his own legs and acknowledge the crowd. Aura.The Scot also made sure to position himself between Myers and Cheruiyot on the start line. A flex, perhaps, but why not? Kerr has the credentials, after all. Former world champion, Olympic silver and bronze, the big dog in this fight.And he needed all of his snarl and bite to survive the three laps of jostling, barging and bumping that followed. The race was slow, too slow. And physical, really physical. Could Kerr - trapped in the pack, pinned to the kerb - deal with that? "As long as you stay on your feet, it's fine," was his assessment afterwards. At the time, Kerr gave his answer as the bell tolled. In a flash, he made his move, bursting to the outside in pursuit of Myers and Cheruiyot, who made theirs momentarily first. With 250m to go, Kerr left them behind. Wightman gamely tried to follow but how do you chase down a man this fast? His brave gamble failed and the bronze medallist from the last two Games trailed home in sixth.By then, Kerr was already celebrating gold, with Myers coming through for silver and Cheruiyot bronze. "I peeked up at the screen, saw I had a bit of a gap, and I felt great," added the Edinburgh athlete, who has been racing at Scotstoun since he was a child. "I was just trying to stay present and enjoy it. I learned how to race on that track - and I've had some pretty bad ones out there - so to really enjoy that last 100m was a really important moment."It was the moment Glasgow 2026 has been building to. The historic, reinstated, Blue Riband event of these Games got a fittingly elite winner. As a student of the sport's history, Kerr will appreciate that. And as a kid who was at the athletics event at Hampden in 2014, he knew how much joy every man, women and child inside this place would derive from every picture he had taken, every word he shared with them, and every scrawl of his name."I have to take my time out there because they've waited and put their hard-earned money to come out and watch me perform," he said."You've got to stay in your lane and realise I'm lucky coming into this championship healthy, ready to go and I'm in the best shape of my life. And to do that in front of a home crowd is very special."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Josh Kerr wins Saturday night scrap in Glasgow

title: Gingers of America - The Scot documenting the redheads of the US
description: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting AmericansImage source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rosalie Moore is one of hundreds of
body: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting AmericansImage source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rosalie Moore is one of hundreds of ginger-haired subjects Kieran has photographedBySteven BrocklehurstBBC ScotlandFor Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade.The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity.His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach.His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap"."I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC. "Then all these people got in touch."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Kieran says he has become quite patriotic for America"I was like 'oh wow, of course, the whole world is in the States'," Kieran says. "It's a microcosm."He says a message from a Native American man who had red hair instantly aroused his curiosity."I found it very interesting and it made me think, 'where on earth did it come from?'"Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Joshua Elliot says his mum's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribeThe cover of his latest book - Gingers of America, external - features Joshua Elliot from the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma.He told Kieran that some of his mother's relatives were German and on his dad's side there were people from England and Sweden, so that could explain where his ginger hair comes from. "My mom's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribe and traditions and I've grown up around it," he said. Joshua knows he does not fit people's expectations of what a Native American should look like, but he said: "Our chief's wife told me it's about your involvement in your community and your tribe, the people around you and what you put back into it."Which I really took to heart." Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Lottie Wahkinney is a Comanche girl, from Oklahoma, with Scottish grandparentsKieran spoke to a lot of Native Americans on his visits and most knew of a European ancestry which could explain their red hair. "The thing that surprised me was how early on there were these Scots and Irish marrying Native Americans," he said.Lottie Wahkinney, a Comanche girl from Oklahoma, has Scottish grandparents, from Galashiels.Her father Jared told Kieran his dad was Comanche but his mum was born and raised in Scotland."That's why my Lottie has a good mix of everything going on," Jared said. "My Scottish grandparents would come over every summer. "On my first visit to Scotland when I was 22, folks were like, 'Where are your moccasins? Where's your headdress?'. "I explained 'I wear Nikes'."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Lakia Jones (right) says all her relatives have long, straight, jet-black hair like her sister Maci (left)While most Native Americans could explain where the ginger gene might have come from, there was one exception - a Cherokee girl called Lakia - whose family knew of no European ancestry."It is a totally different colour of red," Kieran said. "It's deep ruby. That really intrigued me." In the book, Lakia says that all her family, on both sides, have jet-black straight hair but hers turned red during her childhood."Everyone thought, since I was about eight, that I dyed my hair," she said. "And still now everyone's like, 'what hair colour is that?'."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Jaxston Hudson from Birmingham, AlabamaAfter meeting Native Americans, Kieran knew there was something in the US he could explore. Over the next few years, he made seven lengthy trips, often linked to his full-time profession as an environmental photographer.One state he found surprising was Alabama, a place many in the UK associate with racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights as well as its pioneering space exploration programmes."I knew it for racism and Nasa," Kieran said. "In my head it was stuck in the 60s but Birmingham is an incredibly vibrant city."I met a lot of black Americans who had often married someone who is white."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rachel Releford says people think she is her daughter Liliana's nannyRachel Releford told Kieran that when she goes out with her daughter Liliana people think she is the nanny or the babysitter."I'm like, 'nope, she's mine'," Rachel said. "I think you still get some people who grew up with the mindset that things need to be segregated. "Some of my grandparents' friends were a little hesitant when they found out I was dating my husband. They said: 'You're really going to let her date someone of a different race?'"But my grandparents were like, 'Go for it. He's a cool guy, he's a sweet one.' I love him for who he is. He's a great human being."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption,  Henry Davis says he had red hair like his son when he was youngerAlso in Alabama, he met Henry Davis and his young son Henry Davis II.The older man no longer has any red hair but he says he looked just like his son when he was the same age."We're not really sure where it comes from," Henry senior said. "My dad is turning grey now. He'll get some red in his beard, and then it kind of goes grey. "So I guess it's from his side." Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Colton, Bennett, Emmeline, Christopher, Amelia, and Genevieve Smith from Burke, VirginiaAs someone who grew up with red hair himself, Kieran says he is well aware that ginger can be used as an insult.However, he says: "I use the word for its descriptive power because red is the colour of fire engines and blood whereas ginger has a golden tone to it. "You can use it in a kind way."He says the book uses ginger hair as "a golden thread" that weaves together America's diverse and difficult history in a way which shows a connection between people."That's my big idea," Kieran says."We are all made of the same stuff and with the ginger hair it shows."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Cali Trawick has an ancestry that includes Irish, African-American, indigenous American and Hispanic rootsAccording to Kieran no-one exemplifies this better than a young lad named Cali whom he met in Alabama."His background is everything - European, African-American, Hispanic and indigenous as well," he says. "His gran is white but was she unable to get married to a black guy in Alabama - even after the courts had made it legal. "She moved to Georgia and had a family there. It's an incredibly diverse family."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Allison Dubinski grew up in Indiana but says her hair colour is a key asset to help her stand out in the competitive acting world of New YorkIn Scotland, it is thought as many as 13% of the population - about 700,000 people - are natural redheads, a higher percentage than anywhere else in the world.Globally, less than 2% of the population are thought to have red hair but Kieran's research lead him to believe the US figure is higher than that. "We landed on about 4% for the genetic prevalence," he says."If all the gingers in America were gathered in one place, Gingertown would be about 14 million people. "It's a big city. You would see it from space it would be so bright."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Evelyn Lee, from Birmingham, Alabama, used to hate her ginger curls but now she loves them. "I think it's like Spanish princesses' flowing locks - like medieval paintings," she says. Kieran says the big difference between America and other places is that they tend to have really thought about where they come from."Everyone has self-consciously moved from somewhere," he says."And that includes the Native Americans, who have been moved from other parts of America."That's what makes it interesting."He says his book is a road trip through the US trying to find out about the country through this unique trait.Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Keisha Engley grew up in rural Washington State. Her American grandfather fought in Vietnam and met her grandmother there.For Kieran, the recent men's football World Cup got people excited about the US again in a way they haven't been over the past few years because of political divisions.He says he was pleased to see people visiting the US and saying "it is not what I expected"."There's such a lot of amazing people and communities there," he says. "People you might connect with and agree with on a lot of things."I'm quite heartened that the football has revealed that."I feel quite patriotic for America now."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Nicholas Modaressi says his dad, who grew up in Iran, refuses to get his genetics tested. "I'm Persian," he tells his son Nic, who grew up in Maryland

schema.headline: Gingers of America - The Scot documenting the redheads of the US

title: Glen Affric sees first wild-born beavers in 400 years
description: Image source, Trees for LifeImage caption, One of at least two beaver kits known to have been born at Glen AffricConservationists say Glen Affric in t
body: Image source, Trees for LifeImage caption, One of at least two beaver kits known to have been born at Glen AffricConservationists say Glen Affric in the Highlands has its first wild-born beavers since the animals died out in Scotland more than 400 years ago.Findhorn-based charity Trees for Life said there were at least two babies, called kits, known to have been born at Loch Beinn a Mheadhoin following the release of seven beavers in October and a family of four in February.Beavers were first reintroduced to Scotland in 2009, but there have been a number of illegal releases of the animals.Trees for Life has been working on a rewilding project with Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS), which manages the 43,500-acre reserve in the glen.Previously, wild-born beavers were spotted in the Cairngorms following licensed releases of adult animals.Glen Affric, near Cannich, is a large area of woodland, lochs, hills and mountains.Trees for Life said the Glen Affric kits were likely to have been born in May or June, before first emerging from their lodge over the past few weeks.The charity's beaver management officer, Tobias Leask, said: "These beaver kits symbolise a wildlife success story four centuries in the making, and how nature can recover when we give it a chance."Seeing them for the first time is something I'll never forget. It was one of those rare moments when you realise you're witnessing history."Image source, Chris AldridgeImage caption, Families of beavers were released in Glen Affric in October and FebruaryThe 11 released beavers had been relocated under licence by NatureScot from farmland in Tayside.Dr Roisin Campbell-Palmer, head of restoration at the Beaver Trust, said the arrival of the kits suggested the animals had settled well into their new surroundings.She added: "Every reintroduction requires careful planning and close monitoring after release, so it is hugely rewarding to see the animals adapting so successfully."This achievement reflects the commitment and collaboration of everyone involved and provides further evidence that well-managed translocations can support the responsible restoration of beavers across Scotland in line with the Scottish government's National Beaver Strategy."

schema.headline: Glen Affric sees first wild-born beavers in 400 years

title: 'Don't wait until you want revenge' - why prenups are on the rise
description: Celine Tsoi and Charles Mock met two years ago in Goleta, California when she was just 23 and he was 27. Eight months later they were engaged.Friends
body: Celine Tsoi and Charles Mock met two years ago in Goleta, California when she was just 23 and he was 27. Eight months later they were engaged.Friends immediately asked: "Oh, are you getting a prenup?""A lot of things could happen in a marriage and you want to discuss them when you still love each other rather than when things go bad and you want to take revenge," says Celine.These days it's not just the rich and famous; more of us are deciding it makes sense to have a legal agreement that sets out what happens to the money if the marriage ends, with younger couples particularly likely to sign one, even when there aren't great wealth differences to consider.Charles, a nurse, earns more than Celine does as a PhD student, but she had a bit more saved, so the disparities weren't big, but they wanted to face up to important financial questions from the start.She was particularly touched that Charles wanted the prenup to say if they split up, she should have the house.Just having the conversation "can show you what the person you're going to marry is like", she says.Becca expects to inherit a significant amount of property from her parents, which she wants to protect, so in the event of a split, each will walk away with what they started with."It's nice knowing that if anything were to happen, I would just go back to how life was before," she says.Dave, 45, admits it's unromantic but says, given the statistics around divorce, he wants to be pragmatic."A court of law could potentially say, hang on, this guy's earning a lot more than her, he needs to pay her."I built a home for myself. I've built a future for myself, including pensions."Park the emotional side of me loving both her and the kids, I'm no different now to when I met her, and yet she was independent. Why on earth would I have to pay something towards her life in the event of us splitting up?"Couples are also getting married later, points out Julia Rodgers, cofounder of US prenup platform HelloPrenup."You may have some [university] debt, maybe started a business or purchased a home. So you have a lot to protect and to lose by the age of 34," she says.What's become known as "the Great Wealth Transfer" means some members of the younger generation are receiving huge assets to manage. It is often their parents who are the driving force behind ring-fencing those inheritances.And while in the past prenups have been criticised for limiting women's rights, Rodgers argues they have evolved and now benefit women like her by giving them the chance to clarify their rights from the start."We want to make sure we have the honest, open, transparent conversations about life goals, about finances, about roles and responsibilities in the home, so that we can have a long, happy marriage and not end up in that position that we saw our parents in," she says.Celine says most of her friends think prenups are a good idea.It only cost her a few hundred dollars online, but even if she had had to pay lawyers it would have been a worthwhile "investment" in the marriage she says, and less expensive, but probably more important than the wedding itself.Best of all she and Charles have got the "hard conversations" out of the way."We haven't had a single argument about finances," she says.

schema.headline: 'Don't wait until you want revenge' - why prenups are on the rise

title: Remains of Roman port found behind woman's home in East Yorkshire
description: Figure caption, Twelve Roman buildings discovered beneath woman's paddockByJosh Gorroño Chapmanin BroughThe remains of what is believed to be a Roman
body: Figure caption, Twelve Roman buildings discovered beneath woman's paddockByJosh Gorroño Chapmanin BroughThe remains of what is believed to be a Roman port have been dug up on land behind a woman's home.Archaeologists said they had found evidence of 12 buildings beneath a paddock close to the Humber estuary, in Brough, East Yorkshire.Melanie Stanford, who owns the land, said it had come as a complete surprise to learn of the scale of the Roman settlement.Dr Peter Halkon, site director, said the town was ideally located as a trading point, with access to York and the European continent.Image source, Josh Gorroño Chapman/BBCImage caption, Dr Peter Halkon says Brough was ideally located as a trading pointBrough is thought to be on the site of Petuaria, the tribal capital of the Parisi, who lived in eastern Yorkshire during the Roman period.Halkon, 70, is leading the community dig for the Petuaria ReVisited Project, external, which was set up in 2018 to shed more light on the town's Roman past.He said the buildings would likely have been used to store goods taken off ships.Other artefacts found there included pottery, animal bones and oyster shells."The Romans were incredibly fond of oysters," he said.Roman walls in the area have been known about since the 1930s, but digs in recent years have led to new discoveries, including a Roman forum and a theatre.Image source, Josh Gorroño Chapman/BBCImage caption, Archaeologists made the discovery close to the Humber estuaryStanford said she was approached for permission to carry out a dig after ground-penetrating radar revealed the buildings."I said yes, let's see what's there."It's fascinating – I'm loving coming down here. I'm not doing the digging, I just enjoy watching."I'm learning more now and it's really exciting," she added. "With 12 buildings they might be coming back next year to do some more."Volunteer James Newbound, who is studying archaeology at university, said the experience had been really enjoyable."Once you get the bug, you just have to keep going, because it's stuff that's never been seen since it was buried."Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Remains of Roman port found behind woman's home in East Yorkshire

title: Fans praise 'mature' Tom Holland Spider-Man performance
description: Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superher
body: Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.The reviews from critics have been largely positive.Many critics have welcomed the film-makers' decision to scale back from the multiverse seen in No Way Home, in favour of a more personal, character-centred story. The Telegraph's Robbie Collin called it, external "the best Spider-Man film since the Tobey Maguire era", and praised the relationship between Holland and Zendaya, who create a "real yearning and perplexity" that we have not seen previously in the dynamic between their characters.In his review for The Wrap, William Bibbiani, external described it as the strongest entry in Holland's Spider-Man series, applauding its emotional focus and character-driven storytelling, and praising its "wonderful, propulsive quality".Meanwhile, Empire's John Nugent awarded the film four stars, external, declaring the web-slinging hero is "still Marvel's ace in the pack", and in its five-star review The Standard said the film had "verve, intelligence and above all, heart".However, others have been more reserved.The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw declared, external that Zendaya "saves this film" from "silliness and the generic déjà vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it".This opinion was supported by David Rooney in the Hollywood Reporter, external, who wrote that the film "chugs along satisfyingly even with the occasional patch of sluggishness and the usual overly convoluted plot contortions".He adds: "As much as the movie revels in the thrill of Spidey swinging between skyscrapers with erratic command of his shooters, the more intimate scenes with MJ and Ned are what supplies the emotional charge."Danny Leigh of the Financial Times awarded the film three stars, external, praising the chemistry between Holland and Zendaya but criticising the film's insistence on falling back on CGI-heavy action sequences.But that is just what the critics say. What do audiences think?Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.Ten years and multiple other blockbusters later, there is an ever-growing speculation that their futures now lie away from the MCU.Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, external with Josh Horowitz, Holland hinted that a new chapter was on the horizon, albeit not clarifying when."It's going to change, for sure", he said."There is a whole plan that we have been working on since, I would say, Spider-Man No Way Home."I have a really clear vision to the passing on of the baton, and I think it is really exciting."Zendaya and Tom Holland's decade-long Spider-Man romance in picturesAs for Zendaya, she has hinted previously that she is planning on taking a career break at the end of 2026, after a busy schedule that included the promotion of her films The Drama, The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Dune: Part Three.Earlier this year Zendaya told Elle, external that "I think that after this, I'm going to have to take a little bit of a break".She backed this notion up when asked about her future plans, external by Entertainment Tonight at the NYC premiere of The Odyssey, replying, "Oh, girl, nothing. Just mind my business!".

schema.headline: Fans praise 'mature' Tom Holland Spider-Man performance

title: 'We are not lonely': Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle
description: Image source, @lanasololife/@dramafreediaries/@devonandwilloImage caption, Content creators sharing the peace of solo living is making the rounds on s
body: Image source, @lanasololife/@dramafreediaries/@devonandwilloImage caption, Content creators sharing the peace of solo living is making the rounds on social mediaByYang TianIt's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven.What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV.The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night."At the centre of the video – which has amassed seven million views on TikTok – is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto. In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night. Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess.For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years.Alone, but not lonelyImage source, @lanasololifeImage caption, Lana Isa says her videos show her real life and were never intended to "romanticise having no friends"After switching several high schools, enduring Covid isolation during her college years and moving across the country following her first heartbreak, Isa found herself forced to adjust to living alone with no close friends."People don't talk about having no friends a lot... I think it's still what people would consider embarrassing or a little taboo," she says.When she started sharing the friendlessness of her circumstances on social media, an audience began to connect. Her initial following of around 2,000 followers on TikTok swelled to more than 175,000 in the span of eight months."It was eye-opening to see other people who are living the same situation that I've been… and to feel like I could kind of relate to people for the first time in a while."And relate they did. Isa's comments section filled with people bonding over similar experiences of living alone or having no friends, and finding comfort in "feeling seen".Figure caption, Alone not lonely: Meet the women building community through solitudeAs with most trends online, curiosity quickly turned to backlash. Isa and similar creators were dubbed "loneliness influencers", with some framing them as part of a new demographic of sad, lonely, childless women in crisis. Others accused them of romanticising self isolation and encouraging an "air of cosy defeatism" by shunning social connections.But their reels paint a lifestyle that may be more relatable than many would care to admit. These women take themselves on solo dates, embark on spontaneous road trips, and even push through the awkwardness of attending parties alone.Destigmatising lonelinessFor Devon Noehring, a full-time content creator and self-proclaimed introvert based in Phoenix, Arizona, it's been "frustrating" to see her solo weekends cooking and lounging at home with her dog reduced to a symptom of female loneliness."It's the exact opposite intention of our videos," she says. "I just hate the stigma of alone equalling lonely."While Noehring does have a close group of friends, growing up she always felt "ashamed" of being the quiet girl with social anxiety. It wasn't until she confessed her insecurities online that she discovered a following of fellow introverts who identified with her struggles."Being alone is where I feel my most free and most like myself," she says. "That's how I recharge, and I feel very proud of myself for being independent and doing things alone… I think it's something that should be celebrated."Image source, @devonandwilloImage caption, Devon Noehring says her content is about prioritising her peace and asks, "What about this is sad to you?"Some health researchers have been working to "destigmatise loneliness" by differentiating between chronic loneliness forced by circumstance and those who have agency to choose to live and spend time alone."Everybody's lonely at some point, but some people are not OK admitting that," says Professor Melody Ding, an epidemiologist researching social connection and loneliness at the University of Sydney. "That can create this false expectation that you have to be socially happy and connected all the time."But she cautions that while influencers can make being alone look "really appealing", humans still need social connection and it can be detrimental to one's mental and physical wellbeing to be stuck in a cycle of intense isolation."We're a social species," says Ding. "We survive better with companionship, with people around us."She acknowledges that people's social needs vary at different stages of life, but Ding's hope for those who have lost relationships is that they can eventually "de-emphasise" the friendless aspect of their lives and forge new social bonds."It's important we have people in our life and it's important these relationships are positive and nourish our lives," Ding adds.'We want to find people we relate to'Even in moments when they do feel lonely, these women say loneliness doesn't define their lives, nor do they aspire to remain permanently friendless."We never describe ourselves as lonely," says SJ Hoadley, who works as a cleaner in the UK and began documenting her own solo living after discovering Isa's videos. "I think sometimes my lack of friends tends to bother the people around me more than it bothers me."After leaving a seven-year abusive relationship, she moved to a new area where she knew no one and was confronted with having to rebuild her life. Despite the initial "shock", she eventually started "enjoying and embracing that independence" and "getting to feel comfortable with my own company".Image source, @dramafreediariesImage caption, SJ Hoadley calls herself an "accidental influencer" and never expected to gain such a huge followingIn a social media ecosystem that thrives on flooding our feeds with aspirational living and a perennial state of FOMO (fear of missing out), the rise of solo living influencers can be validating for those who see themselves reflected in the lifestyle, says Dr Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch at the University of Connecticut who specialises in how humans build community online."There's been this kind of long growing backlash against the idea that we're seeing everybody's perfect life, their highlight reel," she says.Oeldorf-Hirsch believes the appeal of solitude content is filling a social need for the creators and their audience, providing some "balance" against the dominance of hyper-glamourised influencer culture."We're kind of trending towards these influencers that are more authentic, living their true life," she says. "We just want to find people we relate to."Hoadley has seen her following surge at times by tens of thousands per day, while Noehring's videos have garnered millions of views across her channels.Those online connections have made Hoadley excited for a future where she finds a "little group of girlfriends". Noehring hopes to one day organise a real world meet-up with her virtual community, and Isa says the support has given her the "push" she needed to start thinking about making friends again."I think that what all the content is saying is: find your path," says Hoadley. "It doesn't have to be this one-size-fits-all that we keep getting pushed on social media."

schema.headline: 'We are not lonely': Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle

title: Joe Root in 'very different place' over England Test cricket captaincy
description: England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the rol
body: England's Joe Root is ready to embrace his second stint as Test captain, saying he is in a "very different place" to when he stepped down from the role four years ago.First appointed captain in 2017, Root led England in a record 64 Tests and oversaw a record 28 wins as skipper before stepping down in April 2022 following a 10-wicket defeat by West Indies.At that time, England had won just one of their past 17 Tests, including a 4-0 Ashes humbling away in Australia, while also navigating Covid restrictions, with Root admitting the job "took its toll" on his health."It had become a very unhealthy relationship, the captaincy and me. I couldn't leave it at the ground any more, it was coming home," Root said in June 2022."As soon as I made the decision, I knew it was the right thing to do. I felt like a big weight had been lifted."Root has sparkled since relinquishing the captaincy, averaging over 54 since June 2022 compared to an average of 46.44 in the five years prior and scoring 16 of his 41 Test centuries.However, he told BBC Sport he had no doubts when he was offered the opportunity to return to the role by incoming head coach Stephen Fleming, adding the New Zealander's appointment was a big factor in his decision.Sheffield-born Root, 35, will begin his second stint as full-time captain against Pakistan at Headingley on 19 August, with Fleming joining up with the team ahead of December's tour of South Africa. "It's one of the greatest honours you could wish to have. I'm very excited by it," Root, who filled the role on an interim basis in June when then captain Ben Stokes missed the second Test against New Zealand following an incident at a nightclub, told BBC Sport. "I'm in a very different place to the last time I did it with a team in a very different position."On Fleming, who, like Root, holds national records for matches and wins as Test captain, he added: "I've admired him from afar, first as a player and recently as a coach. To get the chance to work together is going to be great fun."Once I'd spoken to Stephen about it and saw his energy and excitement for it and saw we're very aligned on it, I got excited very quickly."Root and Fleming inherit a side in disarray, with series defeats in Australia and at home by New Zealand - which brought criticism of England's carefree playing style - coupled with a run of off-field disciplinary issues bringing the Bazball era to a disappointing conclusion when captain Stokes retired in June and coach Brendon McCullum was sacked a fortnight later.The duo had previously overseen a resurgence in the Test side, winning 10 of their first 11 matches, and Root hopes he and Fleming can take inspiration from their tenure, rather than starting from scratch."Hopefully we can work and build on a lot of the good things that have happened over the last four years," Root said."I think Brendon and Ben did a brilliant job, in many ways, of turning things around and getting us in a position where hopefully now we can carry that forward in a slightly different way."Expanding on his approach to his second captaincy in an in-house interview with the England & Wales Cricket Board, Root said: "The last four years have been the most fun I've had in professional cricket and a big part of that was down to the way they [McCullum and Stokes] got me to see the game."Clearly, the last little while is probably what's fresh in everyone's mind but you're looking at a four-year period where we did a lot of amazing things. I've taken a lot from that and I feel it will be a big part of how I want to approach things moving forward as a leader of this team."The thing that stands out the most for me is the shift in mindset that was created around how we want to play the game - trying to strip the fear away from things, make sure guys feel that they can really just allow their talent to come out as frequently as possible and in big moments in games. The more that can happen, the better."If we can do that alongside recognising when the right time is to put pressure back on teams, or when the right time is to soak it up and to maybe play situations slightly differently, become a little bit smarter in certain areas, then I think we'll be a very formidable team and a very difficult team to break down and to beat."

schema.headline: Joe Root in 'very different place' over England Test cricket captaincy
